# RequestFox

> RequestFox is a free browser extension for Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox that records every API call a web app makes while you test it, and automatically flags failed (4xx/5xx), slow, duplicate and retried requests, N+1 bursts, GraphQL and JSON-RPC errors returned with a 200 OK, and 401s caused by an expired token. It can replay, mock and export any request, and generate tests and load-test scripts from recorded traffic. It needs no account, has no server, and keeps all recorded data on the user's own device. Current version: 2.5.0 (updated 2026-11-19).

Key facts:

- Type: browser extension (Chrome side panel, Firefox sidebar). Price: free, with no paid tier. Source code: MIT licence; repository not public.
- Recording: fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frames (Socket.IO frames read as events) and Server-Sent Events, across tabs, iframes and popups, including responses served by a service worker. Each call is listed the moment it starts. Live streams (SSE, NDJSON, token streams; read with fetch, XMLHttpRequest or EventSource) show their events as rows while open and keep the newest ones within the body limit, with error events, a missing end marker and long pauses flagged; gRPC-Web and Connect server streams are kept the same way.
- The log: cards or a table (one line per call, sortable, with columns that read a value from each JSON response), Group by host, and a session Overview (counts, status families, slowest calls, findings by kind, hosts). Up to five requests stay open in Compose at once.
- Detection: failed, slow, duplicate and retried requests; N+1 bursts (paths grouped into templates like /products/{id}/reviews); errors inside a 200 OK (GraphQL, JSON-RPC); 401/403 caused by an expired JWT (decoded locally, times only); API contract drift (a response's JSON shape changing); per-endpoint checks including JSON Schema; GraphQL responses checked against a loaded schema; XPath checks on XML (SOAP) responses. Every finding has a stable code (such as RF-FAILED-5XX) with an offline explanation. Each flagged call links to the user action (click or form submit) that triggered it, and failures are explained in plain words.
- Log table and Overview extras: Add column (a value from each JSON response by a path) and Columns (show, hide, reorder, up to four response columns, saved per site); Copy as Markdown (calls named by host and path only) and a Calls over time chart in the Overview.
- Responses: Hex view (offset, hex, ASCII; 32 KB drawn at most) with Copy as base64; a JSON list of objects as a Table with sort and Copy as CSV; a web address in a response opens as a new request in Compose (Open as request).
- GraphQL in Compose: subscriptions over graphql-transport-ws or graphql-ws, events listed live and checked against the loaded schema; custom scalars that declare @specifiedBy are checked by it.
- Suites: Run options (wait between steps 0-60 s, 1-100 runs, stop at the first failure), carried by Export as CI config and overridden by the CLI's --delay-ms, --bail and --iterations. Collections and folders can pin a Default environment.
- MCP control (off by default): an AI agent you run locally can drive RequestFox through `node requestfox-ci.mjs mcp --http <port> --control` (the server is inside the one-file CLI the panel hands out: Settings, MCP control, Download the CLI; 21 extra tools: recording, calls, replay, send, mock and fail rules, rule sets and mock sets, saved requests and suites, exports, clear log, delete collection; throttle is Chrome only). RequestFox runs no AI model. One-time pairing code, 127.0.0.1 only, never the cookie jar, vault, secret variables or OAuth tokens; sending, replaying, deleting and clearing wait for the user's click; at most 120 tool calls a minute.
- Recording options: record the same site in other browser windows (opt-in) and Show page files (scripts, styles, images, fonts; off by default).
- Search: free text, field tokens such as status:500 and host:api.example.com, and a leading "-" to leave matching requests out.
- Testing: replay or edit-and-replay recorded requests; compose requests with environments, {{variables}}, auth helpers (Bearer, Basic, Digest, API key, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE and device code, OAuth 1.0a, JWT Bearer signing, AWS Signature v4, HMAC) and saved collections, sent through the page with its own cookies while recording, or from the extension itself (no page cookies) when nothing is recording or the page's CORS blocks it; chain saved requests into suites with pass/fail per step and data-driven runs. Pre-request and post-response scripts run in Chrome only, in a sandbox.
- Mocking and rules: rules that make a matching endpoint fail, slow down, pause for editing, or return a chosen status and body, without backend changes. Rule sets and mock sets stay on with nothing recording (optional site access, asked per set). A recorded call is mocked from its card: Mock opens a dialog with its status and body to change, then the card says Mocked. In Chrome, rewrite the request or the response with a script; WebSocket message rules drop or change text messages (Chrome and Firefox). In Chrome, Slow down the whole tab (Slow 3G, Fast 3G, 4G, offline or custom) uses the optional debugger permission and shows Chrome's own debugging bar.
- Cookie jar: per site, off until turned on, for the requests RequestFox itself sends; the browser's own cookies are never sent or changed, and cookie values are never exported or logged. Importing the browser's cookies for a site asks for an optional cookies permission.
- Protocols: the QUERY method; gRPC-Web and Connect with the user's own .proto files (own parser); SOAP with WSDL import (including schemas split over files) and an XML tree.
- Import: Postman Collection v2.0/v2.1, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch, Thunder Client, OpenAPI 3, Swagger 2, HAR, cURL, WSDL and .env files; from a file, several files or a folder (batch import with one summary), or Import from URL (the browser asks for access to that one site).
- Export: self-contained HTML report, HAR, CSV, session JSON, Postman Collection, OpenAPI 3.0, code in 15 languages (cURL for bash and Windows cmd, PowerShell, fetch, Node.js, Python, HTTPie, Go, Java, C#, PHP, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, Rust); Playwright and Cypress tests; GitHub and Linear issues pre-filled with a Markdown repro; collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch (secrets become empty variables); the saved collections as one API docs page (Export docs, HTML, no script).
- Examples and notes: save a response as an example; notes on requests, collections and folders.
- Advice: caching and compression advice on responses, and a check that a response stays the same as last time.
- WebSocket client: connects to any ws:// or wss:// server, with a Socket.IO mode.
- MCP server tester: Compose connects to an MCP server over Streamable HTTP (MCP 2026-07-28, and 2025 servers through initialize), lists its tools, resources and prompts, and calls one from a form built from its input schema. RequestFox contains no AI model and no AI code: it only sends the JSON-RPC requests the user picks and shows the responses; a server's request for a model completion is declined.
- LLM calls: a call whose response is OpenAI-style, Anthropic or Gemini shows the model, the token counts and the stop reason that response itself gives; no cost estimates. Like the MCP tester, it only tests and inspects other services.
- Command line (Node, one file, downloaded from the panel): assert (checks), diff, conform (traffic vs an OpenAPI spec), probe (negative tests made from an OpenAPI spec, sent to a local API), mock (a local mock API from a spec or a session; --dynamic varies responses, --seed repeats them), loadtest; docs (the API docs page from a workspace folder); explain (why a finding code is flagged); device-login (OAuth device code); --http2 on assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe (no quiet fall-back to HTTP/1.1; HTTP/3 is out of scope); --cookie-jar and --baseline (fail only on new findings); JUnit output. Every command, flag and config field, and the exit codes (0 passed, 1 failed, 2 could not run): https://requestfox.accessisight.com/cli.html
- Load testing: generates k6, JMeter (.jmx), Gatling (.scala) and Locust (.py) scripts from a recorded session, using each endpoint's measured p95 latency as its threshold.
- Privacy: no account, no analytics, no telemetry; Authorization headers, cookies, secret-shaped fields and the page address are redacted by default in views and exports; site access is requested only when recording starts, or for the sites involved when Compose sends or a test suite runs with nothing recording.
- Languages: 14 (English, Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, Turkish, Chinese (Simplified)).
- Compared with the Chrome DevTools Network panel: DevTools lists every resource live, throttles the whole page with nothing to allow, and leaves the judging to the user; RequestFox flags problems automatically, keeps session history for comparing runs, and supports checks and mock rules. Both show an open stream's events live; RequestFox also judges them and keeps them in History.
- Compared with Postman and Bruno: RequestFox covers composing requests, environments and collections, and additionally records the real calls a web app makes in the browser. While recording it sends through the page; with nothing recording, Compose sends from the extension directly, like a standalone client; when an API blocks the page's origin (CORS), Compose can send from the extension instead, after a click, using the site access allowed at Start and without the page's cookies, a step standalone clients do not need. It has no cloud workspace or team sync. It exports collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch.
- Compared with Insomnia and Hoppscotch: both are API clients you build requests in (Insomnia a desktop app with plugins and Local Vault, Git or cloud storage; Hoppscotch on the web, desktop or CLI, self-hostable, with Socket.IO and MQTT clients). RequestFox records the calls a web app makes and flags problems; it imports collections from both and exports for both. RequestFox has no MQTT client.
- Compared with Requestly: Requestly offers a wider set of always-on traffic rules (redirects, script injection); RequestFox focuses on judging the calls (flags, checks, timing, the code and click behind each call).

The full text of every page, in one file: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/llms-full.txt

## Product

- [RequestFox: API Tester & Network Monitor, Chrome and Firefox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/): Free API tester and network monitor for Chrome and Firefox: records your app's API calls, flags failed, slow and duplicate ones, replays and mocks them.
- [About RequestFox and AccessiSight](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/about.html): Who makes RequestFox, why it is free, and where your data lives: in your own browser, with no RequestFox server, no account and no analytics.
- [API Testing Extension FAQ: Chrome and Firefox · RequestFox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/faq.html): Straight answers about testing APIs in the browser: which tool fits, finding failed or slow calls, GraphQL errors in a 200, mocking, exports and privacy.
- [RequestFox Features: Record, Flag, Mock and Test APIs](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/features.html): Everything RequestFox does in your browser: record fetch, XHR, WebSocket and SSE, flag broken calls, replay, mock, rewrite, check contracts, export tests.

## Guides

- [RequestFox CLI: Commands, Flags, Config and Exit Codes](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/cli.html): Every command, flag and config field of requestfox-ci.mjs, the one-file RequestFox command line for CI, its exit codes and how to download it.
- [Why an API Call Returns 401: Spot an Expired Token](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-401-expired-token.html): Find out if a 401 or 403 comes from an expired bearer token, see when the token ran out, and let Compose renew it before it does, in Chrome or Firefox.
- [How to Run API Checks in CI From Saved Requests](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-api-checks-in-ci.html): Export a RequestFox suite as a CI config, download the one-file command-line tool, and run your API checks in any pipeline with JUnit results. Node 18+.
- [API Testing in Firefox: Built-in Tools and Extensions](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-api-testing-firefox.html): Test an API in Firefox: the Network Monitor's Edit and Resend, REST client add-ons such as RESTer and RESTED, and RequestFox. Dated, with limits.
- [How to Send an API Bug Report With the Evidence](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-bug-report-evidence.html): Copy one failed call as a bug report with its steps, console lines, headers, bodies and a cURL command, or export an HTML report or HAR, secrets hidden.
- [How to Change or Add a Request Header in Chrome or Firefox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-change-request-headers.html): Set, remove or rewrite a request header, a response header or part of a URL for one site, while you test or all the time, in Chrome and Firefox.
- [Copy as cURL and Convert cURL to Python, fetch or Go](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-copy-as-curl-and-convert.html): Copy a request as cURL in Chrome or Firefox, paste it into RequestFox, and copy it out as Python, fetch, Go and other code. Secrets hidden by default.
- [Why Is My API Call Blocked by CORS? How to Find Out](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-cors-blocked-call.html): See which CORS rule blocked an API call: no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, another origin, cookies with *, or a failed preflight, and what the server sent.
- [Find Duplicate and N+1 API Calls in a Web App](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-duplicate-and-n-plus-one-api-calls.html): Spot API calls your page sends twice, and N+1 bursts of one request per id. By hand in DevTools, then flagged for you by RequestFox.
- [GraphQL 200 OK With Errors: How to Spot and Catch It](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-graphql-errors-in-200.html): Why GraphQL answers 200 OK with an errors list, how to spot it by hand, and how RequestFox flags it and fails a CI run on it. Sourced and dated.
- [HAR File Viewer in Your Browser: Open a HAR Offline](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-har-file-viewer.html): Open a .har file in the RequestFox browser extension and read every call, with failed, slow and repeated calls flagged. No upload, no account.
- [HAR to Postman: Three Ways, and What to Remove First](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-har-to-postman.html): Turn a HAR file or a recording into a Postman collection: DevTools cURL, RequestFox, and what to remove from a HAR first. Sourced and dated.
- [How to Import a Postman Collection and Run It in the Browser](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-import-postman-collection.html): Export a Postman collection, import it into RequestFox in Chrome or Firefox, see which tests became checks, and what to set up again before you send.
- [Intercept and Modify API Calls in Chrome, Three Ways](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-intercept-api-calls-chrome.html): Intercept an API call in Chrome and change its response or request: DevTools overrides and Resend, or the RequestFox extension. Steps and limits.
- [Mock an API for Playwright or Cypress Tests: What Helps](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-mock-api-playwright-cypress.html): Mock API responses in Playwright and Cypress with their own commands, and use RequestFox to record real responses and export API tests. Honest limits.
- [Mock an API Response in Chrome: Extension, No Backend](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-mock-api-response.html): Return your own status, headers and body for any API call, or make it fail, slow down or pause, in Chrome or Firefox. No backend change, no proxy.
- [Validate API Responses Against OpenAPI in the Browser](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-openapi-contract-check.html): Validate API responses against an OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 spec in Chrome or Firefox: see which calls break it or are missing, and run the check in CI.
- [How to Record HTTPS Requests in Chrome or Firefox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-record-api-calls.html): Record the HTTPS requests a website makes in Chrome or Firefox: fetch, XHR, WebSocket and SSE, with failed and slow ones flagged. Free, no account.
- [How to Edit and Resend a Request in Chrome](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-replay-edit-request.html): Edit and resend a request in Chrome or Firefox: change its method, URL, headers or body first, or send it again as it was. Uses the page's own cookies.
- [Sanitize a HAR File: What Chrome Removes, What It Leaves](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-sanitize-har-file.html): What a HAR file holds, what Chrome's sanitized export removes, and how RequestFox hides tokens, cookies and passwords before you share it.
- [See API Calls in Firefox, Edge and Safari: Where to Look](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-see-api-calls-firefox-edge-safari.html): Where the Network tool is in Firefox, Edge and Safari, how to read a page's API calls, and which of these browsers RequestFox runs in.
- [How to Slow Down or Cut Off the Network for an API Call](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-slow-down-network.html): Make one API call slow, throttled or fail as if offline, or slow a whole tab down to Slow 3G, in Chrome and Firefox, with no backend change.
- [Test an MCP Server in Your Browser: Tools and Resources](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-test-mcp-server.html): Connect to an MCP server over HTTP from Chrome or Firefox, call a tool from a form, and copy the request as cURL. RequestFox runs no AI model.
- [Test Server-Sent Events (SSE) in the Browser, No Setup](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-test-server-sent-events.html): Send a request to an SSE endpoint from Chrome or Firefox, watch events arrive, stop it, and see error events and early endings flagged.
- [How to Test a WebSocket or Socket.IO Server in the Browser](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-test-websocket.html): Connect to a WebSocket or Socket.IO server from Chrome or Firefox, send text, bytes or events, read why it closed, and record the sockets a page opens.
- [Guides: Record, Replay, Mock and Test APIs · RequestFox](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guides.html): Guides: record API calls in Chrome or Firefox, replay, mock, find duplicate and N+1 calls, catch GraphQL errors in a 200, check OpenAPI, run in CI.

## Compare

- [RequestFox vs Bruno: In-Browser or Git-Native API Client](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-bruno.html): Bruno keeps API requests as plain files in Git; RequestFox starts from what your web app sends in the browser. Neither needs an account. When each fits.
- [RequestFox vs Chrome DevTools Network Panel](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-devtools.html): A Chrome DevTools Network alternative for API testing? What the Network panel does well, what RequestFox adds, and when to use each. Sourced, dated.
- [RequestFox vs Hoppscotch: Two Ways to Test APIs Online](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-hoppscotch.html): Hoppscotch is an open-source API client you can self-host; RequestFox records and judges the calls your own web app makes. Sourced from each tool's docs.
- [RequestFox vs Insomnia: Browser Extension or Desktop Client](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-insomnia.html): Insomnia is a desktop client for designing and testing APIs; RequestFox is a browser extension that flags what your web app really sends. Where each fits.
- [RequestFox vs Postman: A Postman Alternative Extension](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-postman.html): Looking for a Postman alternative in the browser? Postman suits team workspaces; RequestFox records and flags what your web app sends. Sourced, dated.
- [RequestFox or a Proxy Tool: HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman, Charles](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-proxy-tools.html): A browser extension or a proxy app? What RequestFox, HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman and Charles each see and change, and what they cost. Sourced, dated.
- [RequestFox vs Requestly: Two Browser Extensions for APIs](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-requestly.html): RequestFox and Requestly are both browser extensions for API calls. One records and flags them, the other intercepts and rewrites. Sourced, dated.
- [RequestFox vs Thunder Client: Free Limits and Fit](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-thunder-client.html): Thunder Client is a REST client inside VS Code; RequestFox is a browser extension. Free-plan limits, prices and where each fits, from their own pages.
- [RequestFox vs Postman, DevTools, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare.html): Which API tool fits which job: RequestFox vs Postman, DevTools, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch, Requestly and Postman Interceptor, with its own limits.
- [Postman Alternative With No Login: RequestFox and Others](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/postman-alternative-no-login.html): A free Postman alternative with no login: RequestFox, a browser extension with no account at all. Insomnia, Thunder Client and Postman compared.
- [Postman Interceptor Alternative: Record API Calls](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/postman-interceptor-alternative.html): Postman Interceptor hands browser traffic to Postman. RequestFox is a browser extension that records and flags a web app's API calls on its own.

## For

- [For API Developers: See How Clients Really Call Your API](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-api-developers.html): Watch the real calls a web client makes to your API, catch contract drift against your OpenAPI spec, and turn traffic into checks, CI runs and load tests.
- [For Frontend Developers: Debug the API Calls Your UI Makes](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-frontend-developers.html): See which component made each call, catch N+1 bursts and double fetches, mock the states you need, and check timing, without leaving the browser.
- [Manual API Testing Tool for QA Testers, No Code](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-qa-testers.html): A free browser extension for manual testers: see the API calls behind every click, catch failed and duplicate requests, and copy a bug report. No code.

## Optional

- [RequestFox Changelog: What's New in Each Release](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/changelog.html): What changed in each RequestFox release, newest first: new features, fixes and changes to the Chrome and Firefox extension, from its own changelog.
- [RequestFox Privacy Policy](https://requestfox.accessisight.com/privacy.html): RequestFox does not collect, transmit or sell any data. Everything it records stays in your browser, on your device.
